embed_text:
Raising the Bar reforms: Measuring the impact on relative patent scope
Discussion 6

Lastly, from a methodological perspective, this report demonstrates new possibilities in how supervised Machine Learning (ML) methods combined with human expert inputs can be used to improve the quality of assessing patent scope for a large scale policy impact analysis. In fact, there is evidence that relying on previous methods of assessing patent scope such as claim word count may ultimately result in poor accuracy. The implications of poor accuracy can have real consequences as our conclusions would be largely inconclusive.

To enable a highly disaggregated estimation of the RTB reforms' impacts requires a much larger sample size than the original manual validation sample data. For the future, increasing the size of the manually validated sample could turn out to be highly valuable for improving econometric analysis of the reforms. Given that our sample of manually assessed patents did not cover the full spectrum of examination sections within IP Australia, further work may be needed to confirm how the reforms influenced the scope of patents outside of our sample.

Fortunately, the labelled data provided by the manual validation exercise did enable the development of relatively accurate supervised Machine Learning (ML) models to predict relative patent scope for virtually all of the AU-EP-US patent triplet families for which data are available. A crucial step was undertaken to extend and refine the ML models along various dimensions in the implementation of extensive cross-validation and the use of F1-score to arrive at the best machine learning models. In addition, the ML models add a long list of predictive features including extensive incorporation of International Patent Classification (IPC) codes associated with each patent family and extensive hyperparameter tuning.

As noted earlier, the model predictions were driven largely by the various text similarity measures and were not heavily reliant on the International Patent Classification (IPC) codes for accurate predictions. Further exploration could be conducted to better understand whether more nuanced classifications such as incorporating the full suite of classifications or using ML methods to classify the technological scope of patents may yield useful information to improve the accuracy of the patent scope modelling.

European Patent Office

European Patent Office (EPO) data was delivered in Extensible Markup Language (XML) format. XML format allows data to be stored in the form of the string, where symbols allow the reader to annotate parts of the string (sub-strings) as belonging to a certain category. Essentially, XMLs are databases expressed as strings, meaning that all bibliometric and text information related to a patent application will be contained in the string. The inevitable drawback being that a machine must iterate over the entirety of the string to extract relevant information, i.e., completeness at the cost of speed/ ease of handling data. As a result, we were able to cleanly pull all relevant EPO patent claims.

Raising the Bar reforms: Measuring the impact on relative patent scope
IP Australia

IP Australia's archives are presently available as PDF files. PDFs have varying compatibility, de- pending on the year that they were created in and that was used. This means PDFs are not always convertible to TSV or Comma-Separated Values (CSV) format (formats required for machine learning). This process becomes more complicated when the patent claim text contains formulae.

Given that claims data was not easily machine readable via the IP Australia database, we scraped the Australian patent claim data from the public Google patent website (Alphabet, 2023). The process was carried out using the Python package Beautiful Soup. The process was far from ideal and results in claims text breaking down, instances where the text gets converted to non-English or non-sensical words, formulae and chemical structures break down into meaningless symbols and on occasion the text pulled belongs to a different patent application. The data then required further cleaning and management which is described in the later sections of the Appendix.

Another option that became available was to utilise an Application Programming Interface (API) via IP Australia to access the claims text. This was a particularly attractive option as we were able to utilise an official channel for obtaining patent claims text that would be less subject to changes rather than relying either on Optical Character Recognition (OCR) software on the PDF documents or scraping text from a website. Using a software package called Postman, we generated a short Python script to access the Australian Patent Search API. We then tested the output for a couple of example patents and compared the text to the pre-existing data we had scraped. One particular example was patent #2002235407 which is a patent for a Bone Screw which can be found in Figure 12.

Appendix B - Predicting Patent Scope Using Machine Learning Models

In our Machine Learning (ML) modelling, we explored eight supervised learning algorithms, listed in Table 5 alongside the relevant Python modules used. We compared the predictive performance of these algorithms in classifying the relative scope of Australian patent claims using the 500 manually assessed random triplet patent families as the train and test data. We then deployed the best ML Classifier on the full set of patent triplets from 2000 through 2019.

Table 5: Supervised Learning Algorithms.

| Model name | Python module |
|---|---|
| Logistic Regression | Scikit-learn |
| AdaBoost Classifier | Scikit-learn |
| Gradient Boosting Classifier | Scikit-learn |
| Support Vector Classifier | Scikit-learn |
| XGBoost Classifier | XGBoost |
| LightGBM Classifier | LightGBM |
| MLP Classifier | Scikit-learn |

Table 6 lists a series of target variables that we explored. The analysis presented in the body of the report is based on our best ML Classifier using "scope3" as the target variable, which allows us to see how the change in the trend of the proportion of broader patents may be reflected by the change in trend of the proportion of similar and/or narrower patents. In the report, we collapse the three-way relative scope classification into "broader vs not broader" as our focus of analysis.

Table 6: ML models' target variable and best model.

| Target | Definition |
|---|---|
| broader | Broader vs Not Broader |
| narrower | Narrower vs Not Narrower |
| similar | Similar vs Not Similar Broader |
| scope3 | Narrower vs Similar vs Broader |
| scope5 | Significantly Narrower vs Slightly Narrower vs Similar vs Slightly Broader vs Significantly Broader |

Each of the machine learning algorithms is used to estimate our predictions for relative patent scope using generated "features" to classify each class in a given relative patent scope measure for each patent pair considered in the data. The features are generated based on a number of bibliometric characteristics of the patent families such as year of exam request, IPC codes and country of origin, and based on the text of the first claim and/or all claims. The complete list of the features is provided here:

Year of the patent examination request

Indicator if paired patent was filed at the EPO or USPTO

Appendix C - Measuring Relative Patent Scope Using Word Count Differences

To further explore whether word count difference is a relevant method for comparing the relative patent scope of a patent pair, let us look at the reproduced Figure 6 shown for separate AU-EP and AU-US pairs in Figures 13 and 14. The word count difference in these two figures are based on cleaned lemmatised patent claim text. From the figures, it is clear that word count difference may be a reliable method to assess relative scope for a single claim. However, for multiple claims comparison (as shown by the bottom parts of the charts in Figures 13 and 14), the method appears to require additional help from other methods such as supervised machine learning models which we discuss in the next appendix.

Appendix D - Assessing the pre-RTB Downtrend

As shown in Figure 8 and mentioned in the discussion of the baseline regression estimates presented in Tables 1 and 2, the proportion of broader patents has been in a downward trend prior to the RTB reforms. This pre-reform downward trend could be caused by an anticipatory factor related to the RTB reforms or an unknown factor unrelated to the reforms. If the former, then the estimated impact shown in Tables 1 and 2 may be biased downward. In contrast, if the driving cause of the pre-reform downtrend is unrelated to the reforms, then the impact of the reforms has been overestimated.

While it is out of the scope of this report to try to analyse and find the true cause of the pre-RTB reforms downtrend in the proportion of broader patents, it would still be useful to try to get a sense of the magnitude. To do this, we re-estimate the regression model using 2012 as the "treatment"

year. We also restrict the window of analysis to be as narrow as possible, and to start from 2011 and end at 30 June 2013. The idea is that in theory in this window there is no effect from RTB reforms except for the "anticipatory" or the unknown effect.

The result of the regression estimates is summarised in Table 10. As shown in Column (3), the magnitude of the unknown or anticipatory effect is -0.016. Compared to the baseline estimates shown in Table 2 (Column 6) which is reproduced in Table 10's columns 1, the true RTB effect could be as high as 5.8 percentage points reduction in the proportion of broader patents (if the -1.6 percentage points downtrend is caused by anticipatory factors related to RTB) or as low as -2.7 percentage points (if the -1.6 percentage points downtrend is caused by factors unrelated to RTB).

Appendix E - Multinomial Analysis

As a robustness check, we relax the assumption that the relative scope of the patent must be binary or broader or not broader to its international equivalent. Instead, we explore the extent to which the reforms changed the proportion of patents that were similar, narrower or broader in scope.

The figure includes the set of 80,199 patent triplets with examination requests between 2000 and 2019, inclusive. The line plots in the figure indicate that as the proportion of broader AU patents decreases, AU patents became narrower and/or similar in relative scope around 2010 and 2015. We see a gentle upward slope in the share of patents that are similar in scope, yet that trend was present prior to policy change.

These estimates measure the average change in the probability of a patent's relative scope after the enforcement of the Raising the Bar Act. For example, the coefficient estimates for the row 'RTB: Broader' based on the ML Classifier Data on columns (4) - (6) show RTB impact estimates of (-0.030, -0.057, -0.044) for First, All, and Both claim sets respectively. The business environment of patenting firms in Australia
Introduction 1

This report provides insights into patenting trends, the business environment within which patenting firms operate, and the relationship between collaboration for R&D activities and engagement with Australia's patent system. The aim is to provide an overview of the business environment in which Australian patenting firms have operated for over a decade, aiding deeper insights into the structure of innovation in Australia.

This report presents our assessments of the conditional correlations between various business characteristics, such as:

geographical location

firm turnover

size

age

industry

decisions made by firms regarding patent filings, grants, or retirements.

We examine both the overall number of patents as well as the number for each technological field. While there is a considerable body of literature on firms' use of patents, its scope is often limited by the lack of firm-level data, making it difficult to compare across countries and industries. This limits our ability to identify common trends, factors affecting performance, cross-country benchmarking, and the impact of specific national conditions on patenting and business dynamics. Consequently, it hampers our ability to provide evidence for policymaking.

This report aims to address some of these limitations by investigating the characteristics of the firms that engage with the Australian patent system. The findings are derived from analysis of comprehensive microdata in the Australian Bureau of Statistics' Business Longitudinal Analysis Data Environment (BLADE). Integrated data is analysed including the Intellectual Property Longitudinal Research Dataset (IPLORD), the Business Expenditure on Research and Development (BERD) Survey and the Business Characteristics Survey (BCS).

We provide preliminary estimates of the likelihood that a firm engages with the patent system in a given year, based on the business characteristics identified earlier. Engagement is defined as a firm either filing for a patent, being granted a patent, or retiring a patent during a specific year.

We also utilise the Business Characteristics Survey to investigate collaboration network patterns linked to the innovation process and patenting decisions, such as collaborations within supply chains or with universities and research institutions.

It is important to note that our estimates of the relationship between the business characteristics and patenting decisions should be viewed as ranking magnitudes of the strength of the relationships within each characteristic. For instance, the coefficient magnitudes of the industry dummies reveal the industries that exhibit stronger correlations with patent-related decisions, whether they are to file, grant, or retire a patent, and the statistical significance of these correlations.

For example, if we find that age is conditionally correlated with patent filing decisions, it could be due to either patents increasing firms' survival prospects or age influencing the decision to apply for a patent. Literature review 2

There is an extensive theoretical and empirical literature on the economics of patents. This literature includes research on the social value of patents, firms' decisions to patent, and the impact of patenting on firms' performance. Similarly, there is significant literature, largely from management science, on the relationship between innovation and collaboration. Below, we provide a summary of the literature more directly relevant to understanding the business environment of patenting firms.

embed_text:
The business environment of patenting firms in Australia
Literature review 2 > 2.1 Incentives to patent

Theoretical models have been developed to explain why businesses choose to patent their innovations. For example, Horstmann et al. (1985) assert that innovative companies possess confidential information about the profitability of their innovations, and their patent decisions can affect the behaviour of their competitors. When firms innovate sequentially, Bessen and Maskin (2009) argue that patents can be used to hinder potential competitors in their subsequent research. Langinier (2005) suggests that when the leader in a patent race possesses more knowledge about the potential improvement of an innovation, they can strategically choose to patent it.

This theoretical research implies that competition in the product market may significantly influence a company's decision to participate in the patent system. Consequently, market characteristics, such as geographical location, incumbency, and industry, are likely to be linked to patenting decisions. Our findings support this connection.

Empirical studies based on surveys, including research by Sichelman and Graham (2008) and Graham et al. (2009), reveal several key motivations behind firms seeking patents. These motivations include the desire to protect their innovations from being copied, generate revenue through licensing, enhance their negotiation position, and avoid potential legal disputes. Moreover, empirical evidence from Mansfield (1986) indicates that patents are also used to steer clear of the substantial costs associated with imitation or to influence the R&D decisions of competing firms (Palangkaraya et al. 2008). In addition, findings from Hall and Ziedonis (2001) suggest that firms may patent their inventions to minimise the risk of being held hostage by external patent holders. Furthermore, research by Arora et al. (2008) points to another compelling reason for patenting: increasing the overall value of their innovative creations. This body of empirical research aligns with theoretical literature, which underscores the connection between market characteristics and firms' decisions to pursue patents.

Literature review 2 > 2.2 Patenting and firm performance

In another area of empirical research, scholars investigate how patents affect the performance of companies, assuming that the decision to patent is already made. For example, a study by Balasubramanian and Sivadasan (2011) finds a positive link between the number of patents held by U.S. firms and their overall growth. Lanjouw (1998) focuses on West Germany from 1953 to 1988 and concludes that patenting can boost the returns on a company's research and development (R&D) spending by approximately 10%. In the context of France, Schankerman (1998) finds that the returns from R&D activities associated with patents can be as high as 25%. A study by Ortiz-Villajos and Sotoca (2018) reveals that the survival of British manufacturing firms is positively correlated with the number of patent applications they file. Bloom and Van Reenen (2002) show that patents have an economically and statistically significant impact on firm-level productivity and market value of over 200 major British firms since 1968. We build on this research, using BLADE data to explore the relationship between a firm's involvement in the patent system and its growth in turnover.

Literature review 2 > 2.3 Innovation and collaboration

Recognised as an essential driver for economic growth and job creation, innovation is often viewed as benefiting from collaboration with other organisations, institutions, and individuals (Tsai, 2009). In this report, we investigate the relationship between collaboration networks and innovation. These networks involve 12 types of collaboration partners 2 , both within Australia and overseas, resulting in 24 sources in total, as listed in Section 3.2. We examine innovation indirectly through firms' interaction with the IP system, and R&D expenditures and funding. The literature on the relationship between innovation and collaboration can be classified into different streams and summarised as follows:

Network structure and innovation: Studies show that the number of collaborative relationships a firm has is positively linked to innovation, as measured by patents or successful patent applications. However, having structure holes in the network has a negative impact (Shan et al., 1994; Ahuja, 2000).

The business environment of patenting firms in Australia
Data 3

The analysis in this report is based on BLADE business-level administrative records for all businesses that interacted with the Australian Intellectual Property system. The units of observation are firms identified through their anonymised Australian Business Number (ABN). This allowed us to follow them across all the available financial years from 2001-02 to 2020-21. Since financial years, by definition, span across two different calendar years, we will adopt the convention, across the entire report, of reporting the latest calendar year between the two. 3 This does not pose any issues, as all the information we use is collected within a financial year perspective.

The information in BLADE is compiled across a multitude of administrative datasets from several data custodians, which constitutes a high-value and nearly unique setting within the panorama of administrative microdata internationally. Records from BLADE are rich and available at an unprecedented granularity. We have access to an unbalanced (i.e., not all firms are observed in each financial year) firm-level panel across more than 20 financial years with detailed information on firm engagement with IP rights, key firm characteristics, such as location, age, size and industry, in addition to all fiscal records, which also include turnover. Our analysis excludes firms with missing information on business location (0.51%) and/or business industry (1.44%). These sample restrictions only moderately reduce the original BLADE sample size of businesses that interacted with the Australian patent system.

A more significant issue relates to a high proportion of firms in BLADE reporting 2002 as their year of formation. This creates significant challenges when assessing business age. We could not identify the reasons behind the left truncation in businesses' formation dates, but we are wary of their implications. Firstly, we observe a very high concentration of young firms in the first decade of BLADE. Secondly, we only begin to observe a comprehensive distribution of business age according to the young (fewer than 5 years), mature (6 to 9 years) and old (more than 10 years) categorisation from 2011 onwards. For these reasons, our analysis focuses on 2011 onwards. The detailed list of data we use is as follows:

The business surveys available as part of BLADE provide relevant information on the type of innovation collaborations and R&D expenditure businesses rely on. This information, which is unlikely to be captured in administrative records, offers the opportunity to explore innovation contexts of patenting Australian firms. To this end, we utilise survey responses from the:

Business Expenditure on Research and Development (BERD) Survey

Business Characteristics Survey (BCS) 5 : an annual survey that captures business use of information technology; innovation 6 ; and a broad range of other non-financial business characteristics

BCS - Innovation Module (IM): a bi-annual survey on business use of innovation and a broad range of other non-financial business characteristics.

All datasets are available at the Economics Unit Model (EUM) level 7 and can be linked to ABNlevel administrative data using concordance files provided in DataLab. Trends and empirical results 4 > 4.1 The IP patenting system and the business environment > 4.1.1 Trends in patent filings and grants

The left-hand panel of Figure 1 depicts the trends in filed, granted, and retired patents from 2011 to 2021. The number of filed patents has increased between 2011 and 2021, with a noticeable jump of more than 1,000 units in 2013. There has been a consistent increase in the number of patents granted between 2011 and 2016, except for 2013, whereas this pattern inverted in 2017. The notable spike in filed patents registered in 2013 can be attributed to implementation of the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment (Raising the Bar) Act in April of that year. It is important to note that existing patent applications with a request for examination were exempt from the heightened patentability standards introduced by the Act, leading to an increase in granted patents as applicants expedited examination between 2013 and 2016.

Figure 1 | Number of filed, granted and retired patents over time

According to guidance from IP Australia, there is typically a 3 to 5-year lag between the filing date of a patent application and its granting in Australia. Consequently, one would anticipate a delay in the trends of patent grants following patent applications.

The right-hand panel of Figures 1 presents the number of firms involved in patenting over time. While the counts of firms filing and retiring patents have consistently risen from 2011 to 2021, the tally of firms being granted patents follows a cyclic pattern.

The business environment of patenting firms in Australia
Geographical distribution of patents by state and technology field > 4.1.2 Regression analysis

We now delve into our regression analysis. The primary variable we are examining is the number of patents (filed, granted, or retired) reported by businesses observed in IPLORD since 2011. To understand the influencing factors, we consider several covariates, including business age, industry, firm size, state/territory, and year fixed effects, and make the following choices of reference categories:

For business age, we use "Young" (ages 0 to 5) as the reference category, comparing it to "Mature" and "Old."

Regarding business size, "Micro firm" (0 to 4 employees) serves as the reference category, contrasting it with "Small," "Medium," and "Large" firms.

We use "Administrative and support services" as the reference category for industry and "Tasmania" as the reference category for states and territories.

We employed 3 regression models: pooled OLS, fixed effects, and random effects regressions. Here's a brief overview of these models 8 :

Pooled OLS regression: This model considers the same firms observed over time, helping us identify characteristics that are more likely to be associated with the number of patents available over time.

Random Effects regression: This model assumes that unobserved firm-specific factors, like the quality of a firm's management, are independent of the observed characteristics in the regression and help identify firm characteristics that are more likely to be associated with patenting firms.

Fixed Effects regression: This model allows unobserved characteristics to be correlated with the observed ones. It accounts for the fact that firms are different.

Below, we present the results of the pooled OLS regressions for filed, granted, and retired patents. Table 2 illustrates significant differences in patent filing behaviour among firms of different ages and sizes. Younger firms are more likely to file patents than mature and old firms. Additionally, small firms exhibit a lower likelihood of patent filing than micro firms, while medium and large firms are more inclined to file patent applications. Notably, large firms stand out as they display a significantly higher propensity for patent filing compared to smaller counterparts.

However, the industry- specific coefficients become more uniform, suggesting a more consistent pattern of patent grants across industries.

Tables 5, 6 and 7 present the findings of regressions in which the dependent variable is represented as a binary indicator of whether a firm in year it has either filed, been granted, or retired a patent, respectively. Consistent with previous regressions, where the dependent variable pertained to the number of patents filed, granted, or retired, firm size exhibits a positive conditional correlation with the likelihood of a patent being filed or granted. We also observe strong positive conditional correlations in sectors such as mining, manufacturing, electricity, water, construction, and wholesale trade. Notably, the sample sizes for FE regression estimations reduce drastically, indicating most firms' characteristics do not change over time. Nonetheless, the FE models still provide similar evidence of the stylised correlations evidenced so far.

embed_text:
The business environment of patenting firms in Australia
Table 7 | Probability of retiring patents

Finally, we explore the relationship between the growth in firms' turnover and their engagement with the patent system. Tables 8, 9 and 10 report the relationship between our dependent variable, a dichotomous indicator of whether a firm is a high-growth firm 11 , and an indicator of whether a firm, respectively, filed, was granted or retired a patent 3 years before its turnoverbased growth is assessed. All models also account for the characteristics of the patenting firm's business environment. Firm turnover growth is strongly associated with firms' size, age and industry but never with indicators of firms filing or being granted patents at the beginning of the growth period. Interestingly, we observe a consistent pattern where firms retiring patents is negatively associated with future turnover growth. This relationship is worth investigating to better understand the mechanisms producing this consistent negative correlation.

Collaboration is an integral feature of the modus operandi of firms undertaking R&D activities in Australia as shown in Figures 3 to 7. We can summarise the key conclusions from these figures as follows:

In terms of industry, not surprisingly, on average manufacturing firms have the most overseas par tners.

On average, firms in electricity, water and waste services, and in finance and insurance services, have more than 3 Australian partners.

The number of Australian collaborators is evenly spread across firms of different sizes, but micro firms have more overseas collaborators.

Regarding the mechanisms (types) of collaboration, the most types are exhibited by firms in transport, postal and warehousing, in finance and insurance services, and in professional, scientific and technical services. Accommodation and food services, and rental, hiring and real estate services, exhibit the least number of types.

The number of collaboration types is evenly distributed across firms of different size, with micro and small firms exhibiting the greatest number of types.

In our regression analysis, we first consider as the dependent variable a dummy variable taking the value of 1 if the firm has undertaken some form of collaboration during the last two financial years and 0 otherwise as reported in the Business Characteristics Survey. To understand the influencing factors, we consider several covariates, including business age, industry, firm size, and state/territory, and make the following choices of reference categories:

For business age, we use "young" (ages 0 to 5) as the reference category, comparing it to "mature" and "old."

Regarding business size, "micro firm" (0 to 4 employees) serves as the reference category, contrasting it with "small," "medium," and "large" firms.

We use "administrative and support services" as the reference category for industry and "Tasmania" as the reference category for states and territories.

We run a simple logistic regression with coefficients best interpreted as providing a measure of conditional correlation. From column (1) in Table 11, we can infer that by and large, covariates are not statistically significant, except for the positive coefficient on large firms and for a few industries. arts and recreation services

electricity

water and waste services

finance and insurance services

information media and telecommunications

healthcare and social assistance

manufacturing

professional scientific and technical services.

Firms in the Northern Territory are less likely to collaborate.

When compared to micro-sized firms, older and larger firms are more likely to have many collaborators in Australia, whereas smaller firms are less likely to have many domestic collaborators.

Businesses are more likely to have a greater number of collaboration partners in Australia if they are in manufacturing, electricity, water and waste services, information media and telecommunications, finance and insurance services, professional scientific and technical services, and healthcare and social assistance.

embed_text:
The business environment of patenting firms in Australia
Overseas collaboration:

Small and medium businesses generally have a lower number of overseas collaborators compared to micro-sized counterparts.

Older businesses are more likely to have a higher number of overseas collaborators than younger businesses.

Businesses in manufacturing are more likely to have a higher number of collaboration partners overseas, outpacing their counterparts in administrative and support services.

Conversely, businesses in accommodation and food services, healthcare, and social assistance as well as arts and recreation services sectors tend to have fewer international collaborators.

The findings reveal an intriguing pattern: micro firms demonstrate a greater tendency to engage with domestic collaborators than small firms and exhibit a higher propensity for overseas collaborations compared to small and mediumsized firms. Further investigation is warranted to comprehend the underlying reasons behind this counterintuitive outcome.

As previously discussed, our analysis does not provide a foundation to establish a causal relationship between patenting activity and collaboration. It is plausible that patenting activity might lead to subsequent collaboration, as firms actively involved in patenting seek to enhance their R&D endeavours. Conversely, collaboration could result in patenting, assuming that patenting serves as a reliable indicator of innovation. In Tables 11a and 11b, we delve deeper into this matter by investigating the association between collaboration propensity and preceding 3-year and 5-year patenting activities, respectively. The findings indicate a positive correlation between prior patenting activity and collaboration. However, our analysis does not elucidate the potential mechanisms behind this correlation. To grasp the reasons behind this correlation, further research is essential, involving longitudinal data and utilising the patent as the unit of observation rather than the firm.

However, the absence of a statistical relationship doesn't imply that the number or types of collaborators have no impact on R&D outcomes, including those leading to patent filings. Further investigation would necessitate research explicitly modelling firms' decisions to pursue R&D and their corresponding outcomes.

embed_text:
The business environment of patenting firms in Australia
Conclusion 5

This report has shed light on various aspects of the patent system and its interplay with the business environment, as well as the collaborative practices of firms engaged in R&D in Australia. The key findings and insights presented can be summarised as follows:

Patenting trends: Over the past 2 decades, there has been a general upward trend in both the number of patents filed and granted. However, there has been a consistent decrease in the number of patents filed and granted since 2012. While the number of firms filing and retiring patents has consistently increased between 2011 and 2021, the count of firms being granted patents displays 3-year cycles of increases and decreases.

Industry and patenting: Most patenting activities are concentrated in 3 key industries:

» manufacturing

» wholesale trade

» professional, scientific, and technical services.

While patenting activity also occurs in the mining and retail trade industries, it is relatively limited.

Filed patents: Younger firms are more inclined to file patents compared to mature and old firms. Notably, small firms are less likely to file patents than micro firms, while medium and large firms exhibit a higher propensity for patent applications, with large firms standing out as the most active filers.

Geographic and temporal patterns of filed patents: Patent applications are positively correlated with sectors like manufacturing, mining, and wholesale trade, while public administration and safety exhibit a notable negative correlation. New South Wales (NSW) serves as the primary location for patent filings, and the filing year does not significantly affect the process.

Granted patents: The significance of age categories diminishes when considering granted patents. Medium and large firms consistently maintain an advantage in obtaining patents, with industry-specific coefficients showing a more uniform pattern of granted patents.

Geographic distribution of granted patents: Granted patents are more evenly distributed across various regions compared to patent applications, which are concentrated in NSW.

Retired patents: Among age categories, "old" firms show a statistically significant coefficient for retired patents. Small, medium, and large firms retain their significance in this context. The retirement of patents is observed to be more evenly distributed across industries than the filing process, with a notable presence in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) and the Northern Territory (NT).
text:
This report has shed light on various aspects of the patent system and its interplay with the business environment, as well as the collaborative practices of firms engaged in R&D in Australia. The key findings and insights presented can be summarised as follows:

Patenting trends: Over the past 2 decades, there has been a general upward trend in both the number of patents filed and granted. However, there has been a consistent decrease in the number of patents filed and granted since 2012. While the number of firms filing and retiring patents has consistently increased between 2011 and 2021, the count of firms being granted patents displays 3-year cycles of increases and decreases.

Industry and patenting: Most patenting activities are concentrated in 3 key industries:

» manufacturing

» wholesale trade

» professional, scientific, and technical services.

While patenting activity also occurs in the mining and retail trade industries, it is relatively limited.

Filed patents: Younger firms are more inclined to file patents compared to mature and old firms. Notably, small firms are less likely to file patents than micro firms, while medium and large firms exhibit a higher propensity for patent applications, with large firms standing out as the most active filers.

Geographic and temporal patterns of filed patents: Patent applications are positively correlated with sectors like manufacturing, mining, and wholesale trade, while public administration and safety exhibit a notable negative correlation. New South Wales (NSW) serves as the primary location for patent filings, and the filing year does not significantly affect the process.

Granted patents: The significance of age categories diminishes when considering granted patents. Medium and large firms consistently maintain an advantage in obtaining patents, with industry-specific coefficients showing a more uniform pattern of granted patents.

Geographic distribution of granted patents: Granted patents are more evenly distributed across various regions compared to patent applications, which are concentrated in NSW.

Retired patents: Among age categories, "old" firms show a statistically significant coefficient for retired patents. Small, medium, and large firms retain their significance in this context. The retirement of patents is observed to be more evenly distributed across industries than the filing process, with a notable presence in the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) and the Northern Territory (NT).

embed_text:
The business environment of patenting firms in Australia
Conclusion 5

Impact on firm turnover: The report introduces insights into the relationship between the patent system and firm turnover. Firms are less likely to experience high growth once patents are retired, with no statistically significant relationship observed for filed or granted patents. The mechanism that associates patent retirement with reduced turnover growth is unknown and deserves further investigation.

Collaboration in R&D: Collaboration is a crucial aspect of firms engaged in R&D activities in Australia. Various industries collaborate with Australian and overseas partners. Manufacturing and professional, scientific and technical services stand out with the most overseas partners. Our econometric analysis reveals a positive correlation between prior patenting activity and collaboration. However, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Further research is crucial, requiring longitudinal data and a shift to using the patent as the unit of observation instead of the firm to better understand this correlation.

Collaboration and firm size: Micro firms show a notable inclination for domestic collaborations over smaller counterparts and display a higher likelihood of overseas collaborations compared to small and medium-sized firms. Additional research is needed to understand the reasons behind this counterintuitive pattern.

R&D expenditures and patents: R&D expenditure positively influences the number of filed, granted, and retired patents. However, the percentage of R&D funds from the firm's own business negatively affects the number of granted patents. This result is consistent with evidence on the role of patents in attracting investment (e.g., venture capital), but this unexpected relationship between funding sources and patent granting raises

interesting questions that should be explored in more detail. For example, it is of interest to investigate how the link between patenting and reliance on external R&D funding is conditioned by the sources of finance on which a firm relies, such as debt vs equity and government sources.

In summary, the report underscores the dynamics of the patent system, the business environment within which patenting firms operate, and the importance of collaboration in R&D activities and engagement with the patent system. These findings provide valuable insights for policymakers, businesses, and researchers seeking a deeper understanding of the Australian innovation landscape.

Computer implemented inventions: patent trends at IP Australia, EPO and USPTO
Introduction 1

IP Australia (IPA) commissioned the Centre for Transformative Innovation at Swinburne University of Technology to conduct a comparative analysis between computer implemented invention (CII) patenting activities, both the filing of patent applications and their outcomes, in Australia and other jurisdictions (namely, Europe and the United States). This report describes the research methodology and presents the findings of the study.

Patents provide exclusive rights for a limited period for innovators to exploit their inventions in the market to provide incentives for innovation. However, from a society-wide perspective, these exclusive rights can create static deadweight losses (such as inefficient monopoly pricing) which need to be offset against the dynamic benefits of better and cheaper products. Ideally, only inventions with positive net benefits to society should be eligible for patent protection.

In practice, it is often difficult to determine which inventions should be patented. In Australia, for an invention to be patentable it must be for a "manner of manufacture," that is, for an artificially created state of affairs with economic utility. It must belong to the 'useful arts' rather than the 'fine arts' and offer a material advantage in a field of economic endeavour. Ultimately, this test defines how the subject matter in patents is construed in determining its patent eligibility and how the patentability thresholds of novelty, inventive step and disclosure are evaluated. Other jurisdictions have their own definition of what constitutes patentable subject matter.

In recent years, the courts have expanded upon this test to account for technologies not envisioned when the manner of manufacture test was first devised. The recent rapid technological advances in CIIs (sometimes referred to as "software related inventions") have presented serious challenges both to patent offices and applicants across the world. text:
IP Australia (IPA) commissioned the Centre for Transformative Innovation at Swinburne University of Technology to conduct a comparative analysis between computer implemented invention (CII) patenting activities, both the filing of patent applications and their outcomes, in Australia and other jurisdictions (namely, Europe and the United States). This report describes the research methodology and presents the findings of the study.

Patents provide exclusive rights for a limited period for innovators to exploit their inventions in the market to provide incentives for innovation. However, from a society-wide perspective, these exclusive rights can create static deadweight losses (such as inefficient monopoly pricing) which need to be offset against the dynamic benefits of better and cheaper products. Ideally, only inventions with positive net benefits to society should be eligible for patent protection.

In practice, it is often difficult to determine which inventions should be patented. In Australia, for an invention to be patentable it must be for a "manner of manufacture," that is, for an artificially created state of affairs with economic utility. It must belong to the 'useful arts' rather than the 'fine arts' and offer a material advantage in a field of economic endeavour. Ultimately, this test defines how the subject matter in patents is construed in determining its patent eligibility and how the patentability thresholds of novelty, inventive step and disclosure are evaluated. Other jurisdictions have their own definition of what constitutes patentable subject matter.

In recent years, the courts have expanded upon this test to account for technologies not envisioned when the manner of manufacture test was first devised. The recent rapid technological advances in CIIs (sometimes referred to as "software related inventions") have presented serious challenges both to patent offices and applicants across the world. Sherman (2019) has argued that a key reason for this difficulty comes from confusion around the question of "what is software?"

Further difficulty arises from the fact that patent jurisdictions may apply different approaches to what constitutes patent-eligible subject matter and the patentability of CIIs.

With CII's increasing penetration into other technologies and sectors (Branstetter, Drev, and Kwon, 2015), policy makers stand to benefit from a nuanced understanding of how differences in patent standards and outcomes for CIIs affect patent applicant and inventor behaviour. This needs to be understood in the context of significant changes to the relevant legal landscapes.

Construction of CII patent application database

As its first objective, the research project constructs a CII patent application database. This contains a comprehensive record of patent applications filed at IPA, EPO, and USPTO which are identified as CII patent applications. The CII patent applications are identified based on a combination of approaches provided by existing related works including, for example, Frietsch et al. (2015), Xie and Miyazaki (2013), Bessen and Hunt (2007), Chan et al. (2023), Baruffaldi et al. (2020), and Giczy et al. (2022).

Furthermore, the project develops a Machine Learning (ML) model to classify the set of CII patent applications into 2 subsets:

CII patent applications to which (ML predicts) IPA examiners would likely raise an objection in an adverse examination report on the grounds that the patent is not patentable subject matter (PSM). Subsequently, we refer to these applications as "CII-PSM-likely-adverse".

CII patent applications to which (ML predicts) IPA examiners would not likely raise a PSM objection, resulting in a clear examination report with respect to PSM (the application may still be likely to receive an adverse report with respect to other matters such as novelty and fair basis). Subsequently, we refer to this second subset of CII patent applications as "CII-PSMlikely-clear".

In essence, there are 4 steps to construct the CII patent application database:

Identifying CII patents. We identify the set of patent applications based on the approach of Frietsch et al. (2015) of filtering based on a combination of keywords and International Patent Classification (IPC) codes which classify patents into different technology areas.

Construction of the labelled data for developing the ML models. This is provided by IPA and

consists of Australian CII patents for which actual PSM objections were raised in the examination process ("CII-PSM-adverse"), as well as Australian CII patent applications for which IPA did not raise PSM objections ("CIIPSM-clear").

The method does not presuppose or imply standardisation across jurisdictions in the legal standards and tests used to determine patent subject matter eligibility.

A key objective of the research is to investigate the potential influence on applicant behaviour and outcomes of variation in legal standards across jurisdictions, and before and after potentially significant and relevant court cases. These include Research Affiliates LLC v Commissioner of Patents (2014) in Australia and Alice Corp v CLS Bank International [2014] in the US.

To enable this, we need to further distinguish CII patent applications which are at the margins of patent eligibility and likely to have a PSM objection raised. Recent patent studies including Kollmann and Palangkaraya (2023), Kollmann et al. (2023), Giczy et al. (2022), and Abood and Feltenberger (2018) have shown that ML models can be reliably used for identifying and classifying inventions based on bibliographic and textual information in patent documents. Other recent studies which have employed ML models for patent analysis include, for example, Lee et al. (2018), Kwon and Geum (2020), Choi et al. (2021) and Ponta et al. (2022).

This project develops and fine tunes ML models to identify CII patents on the margins of patent eligibility in Australia, and similar applications filed in other jurisdictions, using the seed and anti-seed datasets of CII patent applications described above as training data. The ML model with the highest predictive performance will be implemented on the 'raw' CII patent application database to produce a highly accurate and comprehensive final CII patent application database for statistical analysis. We selected Accuracy, the fraction of predictions the modelling correctly predicted as the primary method of scoring the predictive models.

Similar to the above studies, the development of the ML models primarily relies on features that can be engineered from the textual information contained in patent document titles, abstracts, claims, and, if feasible, descriptions. Additionally, features engineered from bibliographic information of the patent applications will also be considered in the modelling. The ML model development incorporates lessons from earlier work to improve predictive performance, including:

The use of a large training and test sample size

The use of pre-processed words, such as stemmed or lemmatised words according to their parts of speech

Assessment of inclusion and exclusion of specific stop words

Extensive visualisation to detect and, if necessary, exclude outliers

The use of automated hyperparameters tuning.

The consideration of various metrics for the ML objective function

The implementation of multiple folds CrossValidation to ensure robustness.

Impact of changes in legal standards on CII patent applications

The third empirical analysis of the CII patent applications involves a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis of the impact of variation in the relevant CII patenting legal standards within and across the different patent offices. In essence, the DID analysis aims to identify the causal effect of the changes in the legal standards by comparing the propensity of CII patent applications to be filed before and after the changes relative to the propensity of non-CII patent applications.

At the EPO and USPTO and other jurisdictions, the bars for the inclusion and exclusion of CII as patentable subject matter may have been raised or lowered following various court decisions (Ng, 2021). In this research project, the impact of 2 specific court rulings, which are potentially overlapping with respect of their timing and their implications on CII patenting legal standards, are analysed simultaneously:

The Full Federal Court of Australia's appeal ruling on the Research Affiliates LLC v Commissioner of Patents in Australia on 18 November 2014, and

The US Supreme Court's ruling on Alice Corp v CLS Bank International in the United States on 19 June 2014.

The Federal Court of Australia's appeal decision confirmed that Research Affiliates LLC's claims of a computer implemented method (as specified in Patent Application No. 2005213293) are not patentable subject matter. The appeal by Research Affiliates LLC was dismissed - a decision that would have important implications for the patentability of computer-implemented inventions in Australia. Similarly, the landmark 2014 US Supreme Court ruling in Alice Corp v CLS Bank International had a significant impact on CII patenting legal standards, first and foremost in the United States, with potential spillover effects worldwide. The ruling reaffirmed that abstract ideas are not patentable; and any generic computer implementation of abstract ideas is not considered inventive enough as to be patentable.

Due to their occurring in the same year, the impact of the 2 court rulings will be investigated simultaneously using the difference-in-differences (DID) method, comparing the measured change in the outcome variable before and after the court decision of the treated group to that of the control group. Two different outcome variables will be considered: Probability of patent grant and Probability of patent application.

From Figure 8 we can infer that CII-PSM-likelyadverse are less likely to be granted by IPA and EPO than the USPTO. This is true regardless of the sample we use to compute the grant proportion. It is also consistent with our expectation that these 2 patent offices are less likely to grant patents for inventions which lack technical feature or manner of manufacture. For the USPTO, the triplet sample shown in Figure 8B suggests that CII-PSM-likelyadverse patent applications are more likely to be granted (68%) compared to non-CII patents (65%).

It is possible that the higher grant proportion for patents at the USPTO compared to the EPO and IPA shown in Figure 8B is due to sampling variation. For example, one may become concerned with an aggregate grant proportion comparison such as the one above if the alternative to grant contains an outcome that is not actually an outcome, that is an application still pending. In that case, it is possible for a lower grant proportion to be associated with a higher pending rate. This can potentially confuse the interpretation of the outcome measure and its comparison across patent jurisdictions.

In fact, different patent offices may have significantly different pendency periods. Appendix Table A9 shows that while IPA and USPTO have a pendency period (defined as the number of years between grant year and filing year) of around 3 years, EPO has a pendency period of more than 5 years. Furthermore, from Appendix Table A9, if we only look at filings from the early years of the 2001-2020 period we can say that the pendency period at EPO is probably closer to 6 years, since more recent grants are likely those which are granted faster. As a result, if our grant data includes grant decisions made up to the year of 2023 or early 2024 (which is the case for the complete CII patent application database), on average we expect to see "true" EPO grant outcomes only for patent applications filed by 2017 at the latest. For the EPO patent applications filed after 2017, we might see grant proportion to be lower simply because it has more pending patents.

Furthermore, as illustrated especially by Figure A1 in the Appendix and to a lesser extent by Figure 5A and Figure 7A, for IPA the number of CII-PSM-likelyadverse applications prior to 2010 is relatively low.

This low base number results in the computed grant proportion before 2010 that is likely to suffer from small sample bias.

Therefore, in Figure 9, to compare the trend lines of grant proportion across patent offices, we limit the sample period to 2010-2017. The reduction of the upper limit to 2017 is to minimise the likelihood of incorporating truncated/pending outcomes at the EPO and the reduction of the lower limit to 2010 is to minimise the small sampling bias resulting from lower count of CII patent applications, particularly those in the CII-PSM-likely-adverse group.

As seen from the charts in Figure 9, it is possible that the 2014 court decision is associated with a decline in the grant proportion of CII patent applications. In interpreting the graphs, it is important to bear in mind that there is a several year lag between filing a patent application and examination. For example, in the normal course of events there is every possibility that an application filed in 2012 would not be examined until post 2014. That application would then be assessed in accordance with the standard for patentable subject matter as it applied at the time of examination, taking into the decision of Alice (not the standard at time of filing). In Figure 9A we see a decline in grant proportion of CII-PSM-likelyadverse starting in 2013 and accelerating in 2014. The tapering in the rate of decline post 2014 could coincide with applicants becoming more ofay with the legal standards in Australia.

Furthermore, we also note for the USPTO the proportion of granted patent applications does not appear to be affected by the 2014 court decision. This observation appears to be inconsistent with the findings of a recent study which reveal increased first report rejection at the USPTO (Frumkin et al., 2024). There are two possible reasons for the apparent discrepancies. First, first report rejection does not rule out for the possibility of an ultimate grant. Second, it might be insufficient to just evaluate the impact of the 2014 court decision on the probability of grant. The impact may also manifest in the form of more narrowed granted patents. We leave these possibilities for future research.

Determinants of probability of grant

We are now ready to conduct a more formal analysis of the determinants of patent application outcomes. Specifically, we estimate several versions of equation (2) using 2 sample sets: the full sample and the triplet patent family sample. We also split the full sample by patent office to compare how the same patent application characteristics may have different relationships with patent application outcomes in different patent offices.

Before we present the regression estimates, we note that given the discussion in the previous section about potential data truncation (the pending patent outcome problem), all the regressions of the probability of grant are based on the 2010-2017 sample period. This is done to reduce the effect of the much longer pendency period at the EPO resulting in lower probability of grant regardless of CII patent classification.

Table 4 summarises the coefficient estimates of the baseline regression. Comparing across offices, we can see that the conditional probability of an application being granted at IPA and EPO is around 1.8 and 1.5 percentage points lower, respectively, if it is for a CII patent. Given that the unconditional average probability of grant is greater than 40% in both offices, this lower grant probability is relatively small in magnitude. The other regressors suggest some variation across offices in the determinants of grants. For example, the number of assignees has a strong positive association with grant probability at IPA.

Table 5 presents the set of regression coefficient estimates which allow us to compare results for the subsamples of CII-PSM-likely-adverse and CII-PSMlikely clear. These are estimated using all patent families and the triplet patent families and results are compared across the 3 patent offices. The resulting estimates strongly suggest that CII-PSMlikely-adverse patents are less likely to be granted. The probability of grant is lower by around 11.5 percentage points at IPA, by around 4.6 percentage points at the USPTO, and by around 12.6 percentage points at the EPO. These effects are much more significant in magnitude than the effect identified when we did not distinguish CII patent applications based on PSM criteria. The effects are robust regardless of whether all patent families or the triplet families are used.

The impact of 2014 court decisions on probability of grant

As shown in Table 6, the 2014 court decisions appear to have a significant negative effect at IPA. 4 There is an 11.6 to 12.0 percentage points reduction (depending on if we only look at triplet samples or the full sample) in the probability of grant of CII-PSM-likely-adverse applications at the patent office of Australia. In contrast, the effects appear to be positive at the EPO and USPTO. The positive effect at the EPO is possibly caused by the pending period issue we discussed earlier (that is, applications which are more likely to be granted are granted faster and the fact that at the EPO, the average pendency period is more than 5 years). On the other hand, the positive effect of the USPTO may reflect the difference in the way the USPTO responded to the 2014 Supreme Court decision. As discussed earlier, this finding appears to contradict the findings of Frumkin et al. (2024) who found increased rejection in USPTO first action. We argue that these 2 findings may still be consistent with each other if regardless of the first action outcome, the patent applications were granted in the end. Also, we mentioned earlier that the use of post-2014 filing year to determine treatment period may mean we underestimated the negative impact of the 2014 court decision if patent applications filed prior to 2014 were only examined after 2014. At the extreme, the downward bias could lead to a positive effect estimate. However, it is not clear why the downward bias does not appear to have any effect on the estimates based on IPA data. We will investigate these questions in a future study.

Hence, in this set up, we ask what influences the propensity for patent applicant j to file (within the same patent family) for patent protection in IPA after he/she filed for patent protection at the USPTO (or EPO). The key determinant variable that we want to investigate is the CII classification status as shown in a simple linear regression equation below:

In the above equation, CIIi=1 if the patent application i is for a CII and CIIi=0 otherwise. Table 8 summarises the average propensity of EPO patent applicants to subsequently file at IPA. Firstly, note that due to data truncation and family ID information, for EPO we only consider the sample period of 2010 to 2017 filing years. As shown in the table, comparing Tables 7 and 8, we find EPO patent applicants as much more likely to follow up their application with subsequent filing at IPA than are applicants to the USPTO. On average, the unconditional proportion of EPO patents subsequently filed at IPA is around 13%, slightly more than double the proportion for USPTO patent applicants. More interestingly, in contrast to USPTO applicants, EPO applicants of CII-PSM-likelyadverse applications appear to be more likely to file subsequently at IPA than applicants of CIIPSM-likely-clear. A more in-depth analysis (out of the scope for this report) is required to understand the possible drivers of this result. However, a plausible interpretation is that applicants with CII patent applications more likely to be considered as "software as such" by EPO patent examiners may think they have an improved chance if they also try to get patent protection at IPA.

The more interesting point to note is obtained by comparing estimates from across the different subsamples. For example, the number of assignee countries associated with a patent is often considered an indicator of the potential technology and economic value of the invention. In our results, the more assignee countries associated with a patent, the more likely that patent protection is likely to be sought for a "CII-PSM-likely-adverse" invention in Australia following its filing at the USPTO. One additional assignee country in the team is associated with an average increase of probability to apply to IPA by close to 2 percentage points. Given the average unconditional probability of applying to IPA for "CII-PSM-likely-adverse" patents is 3 percentage points, this effect is significant in magnitude. In fact, compared to other subsamples, the effect of an additional assignee country is more than twice as large for "CII-PSMadverse" inventions.

Other coefficient estimates in the table show the expected effects. For example, applicants are more likely to apply to IPA if they have applied there before or if the patent application is part of a divisional application. Applicants from leading assignee countries in terms of patenting activities (e.g., China, Japan and Korea) are less likely to apply for patent protection in IPA following their filing at the USPTO.

To assess any potential impact of 2014 court decisions, we conduct a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis with USPTO and EPO applicants' subsequent filing propensity to IPA as the outcome measure. We do this by adding 2 key variables to the same regressions summarised in Table 9 and Table 10. These variables are:

Post-2014: with a value of 1 for all applications filed after 2014, and 0 otherwise 5

Post-2014 x CII status: an interaction term between Post-2014 and CII classification status. We consider "CII" and "CII-PSM-likely-adverse" as the CII status.

Table 11 summarises the main parameters of interest for the difference-in-differences regression based on 2 different sample periods. 6 The regressions include the same determinants shown in Table 8, but they are omitted since they are not our main interest. In the table, Model 1 is based on IPA subsequent filing data of USPTO applicants. Model 2 is based on the data of EPO applicants. In Models 1A and 2A, CII is compared to Non-CII. The estimates for Post-2014 x CII is statistically significant and positive (0.01) for USPTO applicants.

This suggests that for CII applications, compared to Non-CII applications, the 2014 court decisions were actually associated with an increase in the relative probability of applicants subsequently filing at IPA. Qualitatively, this result is robust with respect to the sample period.

We now investigate the impact of the 2014 court decisions on the patent filing propensity of past IPA applicants. For this, we estimate a modified equation (4) as follows:

where, as in equation (4), j indexes applicant, k indicates IPA as the filing office, and t indexes the filing year. The equation is modified such that the dependent variable, yijk , is a binary variable equal to 1 if an applicant who previously filed a CII application at IPA prior to 2014 files a subsequent CII application at IPA post-2014. In the above equation, Post2014t=1 "if filing year " t>2014 and 0 otherwise. In other words, Post2014t indicates the treatment years.

As in the case of equation (4), the main parameter of interest in equation (5) is provided by the parameter of the interaction term Treatedjk× Post-2014, namely β3 . In this case, β3<0 could mean three different possibilities with respect to the impact of the 2014 court decisions: (i) a decrease in the propensity of CII innovation, (ii) a decrease in the propensity to apply for CII patent application (even if there is no decrease in the propensity of CII innovation), or (iii) a combined decrease in the propensities for CII innovation and for filing CII patent application.

Strictly speaking, the setup in equation (5) cannot identify the above three possible interpretations. However, let us further define the treatment groups (indicated by Treatedjk=1) in terms of 2 distinct subsets of CII applicants: 8

Treatedjk=1 for all IPA applicants j who have ever filed for CII patent applications at IPA prior to 2014.

Treatedjk=1 for all IPA applicants j who have ever filed for CII patent applications at IPA prior to 2014 and have at least 1 IPA patent application (regardless of CII classification status) after 2014.

As defined above, the second definition of Treatedjk=1 could indicate whether the estimated impact of the 2014 court decisions can be interpreted as the impact on the propensity of producing a CII invention or the impact on propensity of filing for CII patent protection (given a CII invention has been produced). The intuition is as follows. If the 2014 court decision negatively affect inventor behaviour, then we will see this as a decrease in patent application filing. However, this decrease could be caused by a lower rate of innovation or a lower propensity to file for patent application (even if the rate of innovation is unchanged). The second treated Treatedjk=1 group definition above adds the condition "have at least 1 IPA patent application (regardless of CII classification status) after 2014". This is to control for the "rate of innovation is unchanged". If β3>0 for this subset of the treated group, then we may infer there is unlikely a change in CII inventor to file for CII patent application post-2014. This is because a positive coefficient means if the CII inventor has an invention he or she will be more likely to file it as a CII patent application. In contrast, if β3<0, we have an indication that the propensity to file for patent (and not the propensity to innovate) is negatively impacted. If we know that the underlying invention of the condition "have at least1 IPA patent application (regardless of CII classification status) after 2014" is a CII invention, then we can be more confident to conclude that there is a substitution away from filing a CII patent. However, if the underlying invention is non-CII, then it could mean the rate of CII innovation has decreased (given that the patent applicant has CII patent application pre-2014).

We now focus on the propensity of past applicants who file a subsequent patent after 2014 to file a CII or CII-PSM-likely-adverse application. The results, summarised in Models 2A and 2B, appear to be sensitive to the sample period used. In contrast, the estimates based on the 2010-2019 sample period suggest a lower propensity to file for CII (or CII-PSM-likelyadverse) patents following the court decisions. However, the negative estimates from Model 2A and 2B based on the 2010-2019 sample do not provide any clear indicator of the real reason for the lower propensity. These estimates are plausibly consistent with a lower CII innovation output or a higher reluctance to file for CII patent (even if CII innovation output level is maintained). For example, the estimates in Model 2B show that, among patent applicants who filed CII-PSMlikely-adverse applications prior to 2014, and who actually filed for patents after 2014, there was an 9.2 percentage points reduced probability that the post-2014 application was CII-PSM-likely-adverse. Discussion

The main objective of this study is to provide a better understanding of how patenting for computerimplemented inventions (CII) in Australia differs from patenting for other types of inventions and how patenting for CII in Australia differs from patenting for CII in Europe and the United States. For this purpose, we conducted both descriptive and formal econometrics analyses to evaluate differences and potential drivers of these differences in the likelihood of patent applications being granted and the likelihood of applicants from around the world applying for patent protection in Australia. Included in these analyses is an impact evaluation of two 2014 court decisions which are closely related to the patentability of CII by providing new guidelines on the question of what constitutes patentable subject matter (a "manner of manufacture" in Australia):

The empirical analysis is based on a CII patent application database constructed in this research project. It contains a comprehensive set of patent applications filed at IP Australia (IPA), the European Patent Office (EPO), and the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) from 2001-2020. The total number of patent applications useable for the analysis exceeds 500,000 for IPA, 2.8 million for the EPO, and 10.1 million for the USPTO. 9

Furthermore, to enable us to identify a "true" causeand-effect relationship between CII patenting in Australia and the 2 court decisions mentioned earlier, we classified these patent applications into 3 subgroups: "CII-PSM-likely-adverse", "CII-PSMlikely-clear", and "Non-CII". The first group consists of CII patent applications at each office which are highly similar to patent applications which received manner of manufacture objections from IPA patent examiners. The intuition is that if the court decisions in Alice Corp v CLS Bank International [2014] and Research Affiliates LLC v Commissioner of Patents [2014] did have any impact then this impact should be the strongest for "CII-PSM-likely-adverse" patent applications and there should be no impact on "Non-CII" patent applications. If our impact estimates are not consistent with this intuition, then it is likely that our impact estimates are biased and possibly misleading.

Discussion

Also, to ensure that we are comparing apples-toapples and thus minimising bias, in some of our comparative analysis, for example on the likelihood of grant across the 3 jurisdictions, we restricted the sample to "triplet patent families". These patent families consist of "equivalent patent" applications which were filed at IPA, EPO, and USPTO. In this case, we can attribute any observed difference in their likelihood of grant across the 3 offices to the difference in the offices' patent examination procedures, rather than underlying characteristics of the invention or patent application.

Our main approach is to compare before and after the 2014 court decisions. We employed differencein-differences (DID) where the change in the average outcome for CII patent applications is compared to the change in the average outcome for non-CII patent applications. The change in the average outcome for non-CII patent applications measures what would have happened had there been no 2014 court decision. In the DID terminology, the CII patent applications are in the treatment group and the non-CII patent applications are in the control group.

The first important finding from the analyses is that there is a significant difference in the likelihood of CII-PSM-likely-adverse applications to be granted across the 3 patent offices. 10 CII-PSM-likely-adverse applications are most likely to be granted by the USPTO, with a grant rate of close to 70%. Compared to USPTO, the grant rate of CII-PSM-likely-adverse applications at IPA is almost 23 per cent lower at 54%. The EPO grant rate of CII-PSM-adverse applications is less than 50 per cent of the USPTO grant rate at around 27%. The inter-office difference in grant rates for CII-PSM-likely-clear and Non-CII is much less significant. This result suggests a relatively high degree of inter-office disharmony in determining the patentability of CII patent applications with claims that are on the margins of patentable subject matter.

Applicants in the treatment group not having any invention to file for patent protection post2014 or not seeking patent protection at all, or

Applicants in the treatment group filing for patent protection post-2014 but not filing the invention as a CII patent.

We divided our treatment group into 2 distinct treatment groups according to the above 2 possible reasons. We conducted 2 DID analyses using each of these newly defined treatment groups. We interpret the negative effect for the treatment group defined by reason (1) as evidence that there is a lower number, on average, of CII patented inventions post-2014. In contrast, a negative effect for the treatment group defined by reason (2) cannot be interpreted as a reduced level of patented innovation. Instead, it indicates that when they apply for patents after 2014, the pre-2014 CII applicants are on average more likely to file for non-CII patent applications. 12 Furthermore, a positive effect for the treatment group defined by (2) would negate the possibility that the owners of post-2014 CII inventions may file their applications in different categories.

We found, based on the treatment group defined by reason (2), the 2014 Alice and Research Affiliates court decisions decreased the propensity of applicants to file CII-PSM-likely-adverse applications at IPA by 9.2 percentage points. Previously we found a 22.6 percentage points reduction in the propensity of applicants to file CII-PSM-likely-adverse applications at IPA, focused on the treatment group defined by reason (1). We conclude that slightly more than half ((22.6 - 9.2)/22.6) of the negative impact of Alice and Research Affiliates on the propensity of applicants to file at IPA is due to decreased CII innovation and changes in the patenting strategy (that is, patent applicants filing their invention as non-CII or CIIPSM-clear or no patent filing at all).

Discussion

Lastly, we also assessed the impact of Alice and Research Affiliates on CII patent propensity for applicants to IPA. To this end, we looked at whether CII patent applicants who filed for patent protection at USPTO and the EPO file equivalent patents at IPA. Note that in this case, a negative effect, if any, cannot be interpreted as 'lower innovation'; instead, it is clearly an effect on the patenting strategy. Approximately 3% of CII-PSM-likely-adverse patent applications filed at the USPTO were subsequently filed at IPA. This compares to an overall follow-up rate at IPA for USPTO applications of 5%. Hence, it appears that USPTO applicants for CII-PSMlikely-adverse patents are not as likely to apply for patent applications at IPA as the average USPTO applicant. The follow-up rate for CII-PSM-likelyadverse applications filed at the EPO is significantly higher at 15% and there is no difference in EPO follow-up rate between CII-PSM-likely-adverse and Non-CII patents.

We then compare the follow-up propensity before-and-after the 2014 changes using the same DID method as above. We found that the effect is positive for USPTO and negative for the EPO. However, the magnitude of the estimates is relatively small compared to the baseline followup rates provided above. 14 Hence, the Alice and Research Affiliates decisions do not appear to have changed the patenting strategy of applicants who file CII-PSM-likely-adverse patents at the USPTO and EPO to file associated applications at IPA.

We then compare the follow-up propensity before-and-after the 2014 changes using the same DID method as above. We found that the effect is positive for USPTO and negative for the EPO. However, the magnitude of the estimates is relatively small compared to the baseline followup rates provided above. 14 Hence, the Alice and Research Affiliates decisions do not appear to have changed the patenting strategy of applicants who file CII-PSM-likely-adverse patents at the USPTO and EPO to file associated applications at IPA.
